correctness.rationale: The three exact moments follow by choosing fixed edge sets subject to specified isolated and degree-one vertices. Conditioning on isolation gives G(n-1,m) exactly. The consecutive leaf-mean ratio is 1 at m=1 and decreases strictly through m=B+1 by the displayed positive difference, proving negative covariance on 2<=m<=A. Beyond B+1 the smaller graph has zero leaf expectation; at m=0,1 or m>A one statistic is constant. The sparse limit follows from product estimates and a uniform 1-2/n²+O(n^-3) consecutive-ratio expansion. Actual embedded Python checker passed exhaustive graphs n<=6 and exact-arithmetic tests all n<=84; finite checks are not the universal proof.

originality.rationale: Goldstein–Rinott (1996, §4.2 Eq. 25), inspected in full relevant section, directly supplies the G(n,p) covariance comparator, so the latter is explicitly not claimed as new. Its independent-edge formula does not imply the exact all-m G(n,m) negative covariance sign, exact zero boundaries, strict conditioning-ratio mechanism, or sparse fixed-edge limit. Goldstein (2010/2013) studies a single degree class with independent edges and is likewise insufficient. Six semantic database queries and focused literature searches sought aliases and dominating degree-profile results; the nearest records concern different models or statistics. Historical novelty remains provisional because earlier fixed-edge joint degree-count formulas cannot be ruled out conclusively.
residual_risks: Older exact joint-degree-count and asymptotic covariance work for G(n,m), possibly implicit in a general theorem, may supersede the result.
Bollobás (1981) and some older joint-degree-profile sources were not inspected in full; absence of a search hit does not establish uniqueness.

value.rationale: Degree-count cross-covariances are natural inputs in joint approximations for random graph degree profiles. Fixed-edge conditioning, an important finite-sample model, reverses a classical Bernoulli ensemble covariance sign at precisely matched expected edge counts (m=n for every n>=5). The all-parameter strict sign boundary, conditional-deletion monotonicity mechanism, and sparse leading-order covariance explain a structural dependence phenomenon rather than an isolated routine numerical calculation.
